note: The Gloria Patri, the short hymn of praise to the Trinity that closes the psalms in church services. All the blessed sing it as Adam finishes speaking.
One of the best known phrases of Paradiso: in Italian, "un riso de l'universo", a smile or laugh of the universe.
The apostles Peter, James and John, who examined Dante on faith, hope and love, and Adam, who joined them in Canto 26.

quote: the one that had come first
context: Peter was the first to come to Dante, in Canto 24. Now his light turns red with anger, and he condemns the popes who have followed him.

note: Jupiter shines white and Mars red. If the two planets swapped colors, Jupiter would glow red: so Peter's white light reddens.

context: Pope at the date of the journey, 1300. Peter calls him a usurper: he holds the office before the world, but in Christ's eyes the seat is empty.

quote: my place, my place, my place!
note: The triple cry is in Dante's Italian: "il luogo mio" three times. Commentators hear an echo of the prophet Jeremiah, who repeats "the temple of the Lord" three times against those who defile it.
Rome, where Peter was martyred and buried, along with many of the first Christians.

quote: the Perverse One who fell from here
context: The corruption of Rome is what pleases him.

note: The whole heaven of the saints turns the red of sunset clouds, blushing with anger and shame at what Peter says.
The Gospels say darkness covered the land for three hours while Christ hung on the cross. Dante imagines that Heaven itself dimmed then, as it does now.
The Church, a common image from the New Testament. Peter says the first popes fed her with their blood, dying as martyrs.
The first two bishops of Rome after Peter, in the traditional list of popes. Both were honored as martyrs.

quote: Sixtus and Pius, Urban and Callixtus
note: Four popes of the second and third centuries: Sixtus I, Pius I, Callixtus I and Urban I. The church honored all four as martyrs.

The popes had become party leaders, favoring the Guelphs, who backed them, and treating the Ghibellines, who backed the emperor, as enemies. The right and left hand recall Christ at the Last Judgment, setting the saved on his right and the damned on his left: a division no pope is entitled to make.

Christ gave Peter "the keys of the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 16:19). Crossed keys became the emblem of the papacy, and papal armies carried them on their banners into wars against fellow Christians, such as Boniface's war on the Colonna family (Inferno 27).
The papal seal carried the heads of Peter and Paul. It was stamped on grants of favors and offices that Dante says were bought with money.

Christ's warning in Matthew 7:15 against false prophets, "which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves". Here the wolves are dressed as the shepherds: the bishops and popes themselves.

context: John XXII came from Cahors, a town whose name was already a byword for moneylending (Inferno 11). He became pope in 1316. The journey is set in 1300, so Peter speaks of him as still to come.
Clement V was from Gascony, in southwestern France. Peter foretells him, like John XXII, as a pope who will live off the blood of the martyrs.
Peter takes Rome's rescue from Hannibal as proof that God guards the city, and promises that the same Providence will rescue the Church.

note: Another of the poem's prophecies of a rescuer, like the greyhound of Inferno 1 and the messenger of God foretold in Purgatorio 33. None of them names a person or a date.

Peter orders Dante to publish what he has heard. Beatrice gave him the same charge in the Earthly Paradise (Purgatorio 32–33), and so did his ancestor Cacciaguida in Paradiso 17. The attack on the popes is thus made a duty laid on him by the first pope.
The constellation Capricorn. The sun is in it in midwinter, from late December into January, the season of snow.
The souls of the blessed, who came down to this heaven in Canto 23. They now rise back to the Empyrean like snow falling upward.
Dante's second look back at the earth. The first was in Canto 22, when he entered this heaven and smiled at how small the world looked.

Ancient geographers divided the inhabited world into bands of latitude called climates. The inhabited land was thought to stretch halfway round the globe, from the Ganges to Cadiz, with Jerusalem at its middle. Dante has been carried from above the middle to above the western end: a quarter of a circle, or six hours.

context: Looking west, Dante sees the Atlantic where Ulysses sailed to his death. Ulysses called that voyage a "mad flight" (Inferno 26). Dante's Italian names Cadiz, on the Atlantic coast just beyond the Strait of Gibraltar.

note: A princess of Phoenicia, on the coast of what is now Lebanon. In the myth Jupiter took the shape of a bull, coaxed her onto his back and swam off with her to Crete. Looking east, Dante can see almost as far as that shore.
The inhabited earth, small and flat as a patch of beaten ground. Dante used the same word on his first look down, in Canto 22: the little threshing floor that makes us so fierce.

quote: the sun was moving beneath my feet
note: Dante is in the constellation Gemini. The sun is in Aries, farther west, with the whole sign of Taurus between them, so its light has already left the eastern edge of the world, and he cannot see the rest.

The constellation Gemini, the Twins. In the myth Jupiter came to Leda as a swan, and the twins Castor and Pollux were hatched from her egg. Gemini is Dante's own birth sign, and he has been in it since Canto 22.

context: Dante rises into it from the fixed stars. It is the same in every part, so he cannot tell where he has entered.

note: The plan of Dante's universe: the earth sits motionless at the center, and nine spheres turn around it, each inside the next. All that turning starts in this outermost sphere.

context: Every other heaven is contained by the one above it. This last sphere is contained by nothing physical: it has its place only in God's mind, whose love makes it turn.

quote: as ten is measured by its half and fifth
note: Ten is five times two. As ten gives the measure of its factors, the speed of this heaven sets the motions of all the slower spheres below it, and nothing sets its own.
Time is measured by the movement of the heavens: the sun gives days and years, the moon months. Those are the visible leaves. The hidden root is this sphere, the source of all their motion.

Beatrice turns without warning from the order of the heavens to the disorder of human life. Greed, "cupidigia", is for Dante the vice that most keeps people from looking up: the she-wolf of Inferno 1.
Constant rain makes plums swell into empty, spoiled fruit. So the good will that people are born with is ruined as they grow.
The church set days and seasons, such as Lent, when meat was forbidden. The pious child grows into a man who eats whatever he likes whenever he likes.

Three of the most disputed lines in the poem. Dante's Italian names no one: it says only "the fair daughter of him who brings morning and leaves evening", that is, of the sun. The translation takes her as the Dawn. Others take her as Circe, the sun's daughter in myth, or as humankind, or the Church. The general sense is clear: what starts out fair turns dark.

For Dante the world needs two guides, an emperor for this life and a pope for the next. In 1300 the emperor-elect had never set foot in Italy, and the papacy was, as Peter has just said, vacant in God's eyes.

The calendar of Dante's day counted the year as 365 days and a quarter, which is too long by roughly a hundredth of a day. The error slowly pushed the dates out of step with the seasons, so that January would in time have fallen in spring. That would take thousands of years: Beatrice means "soon", by ironic understatement. The calendar reform of 1582 corrected the error.

A last prophecy of rescue. Dante's word is "fortuna", which can mean a storm at sea: one that will turn the fleet of humankind around and set it on its right course. As with the other prophecies, who will bring it is left unsaid.
